items.stem: What is a parallel circuit?
options: A circuit with more than one path (branch) for the current
A circuit with only one path for the current
A circuit with only one component
items.answer: A circuit with more than one path (branch) for the current
items.markingKey: Components are on separate branches.

items.stem: Explain why two lamps in parallel are brighter than the same two lamps in series with the same battery.
items.answer: In parallel each lamp gets the full battery voltage; in series the voltage is shared, so each lamp gets less.
items.markingKey: full voltage in parallel [1]; shared in series [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a switch in the main part of a parallel circuit turns off all the lamps.
items.answer: All the current passes through the main part; opening the switch breaks the circuit for every branch.
items.markingKey: all current through main part [1]; every branch broken [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas is designing the circuit for the headlamps of a toy car, using a battery, 2 lamps and switches. Describe the circuit, including where the switches go, so that each lamp can be controlled separately and all lamps can be turned off at once.
items.answer: Connect the 2 lamps in parallel, each branch with its own switch; put a master switch in the main circuit next to the battery.
items.markingKey: lamps in parallel [1]; switch on each branch [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun is designing the circuit for the headlamps of a toy car, using a battery, 3 lamps and switches. Describe the circuit, including where the switches go, so that each lamp can be controlled separately and all lamps can be turned off at once.
items.answer: Connect the 3 lamps in parallel, each branch with its own switch; put a master switch in the main circuit next to the battery.
items.markingKey: lamps in parallel [1]; switch on each branch [1]; master switch in main circuit [1] [3]

items.stem: An electrician in Cairo wires the lights in a new flat in parallel. (a) Explain what happens to the other lamps if one lamp breaks. (b) Describe how to connect an ammeter to measure the current in one lamp only.
items.answer: (a) They stay lit, because each is on a separate complete branch. (b) Put the ammeter in series with that lamp, on its branch.
items.markingKey: (a) stay lit [1]; separate branches [1] [2] (b) series [1]; on that branch [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a switch on one branch of a parallel circuit controls only the lamp on that branch.
items.answer: Opening it breaks only that branch; the other branches still form complete circuits with the cell.
items.markingKey: breaks only that branch [1]; others complete [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why circuit diagrams use standard symbols.
items.answer: So that anyone anywhere can read and build the circuit without confusion.
items.markingKey: universally understood [1]; clear / no confusion [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha is designing the circuit for a set of decorative lights for a festival, using a battery, 3 lamps and switches. Describe the circuit, including where the switches go, so that each lamp can be controlled separately and all lamps can be turned off at once.
items.answer: Connect the 3 lamps in parallel, each branch with its own switch; put a master switch in the main circuit next to the battery.
items.markingKey: lamps in parallel [1]; switch on each branch [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia builds a circuit with a 6 V battery and three identical lamps in parallel for a school project. (a) State the voltage across each lamp if the supply is 6 V. (b) Explain why houses use parallel rather than series circuits for lighting.
items.answer: (a) 6 V (b) Lights can be switched independently and one failing does not switch the others off; each gets full mains voltage.
items.markingKey: (a) each branch has supply voltage: 6 V [1] (b) independent switching [1]; one fails others stay on / full voltage [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah is designing the circuit for the lights on a bicycle (front and back), using a battery, 2 lamps and switches. Describe the circuit, including where the switches go, so that each lamp can be controlled separately and all lamps can be turned off at once. Explain where to place an ammeter to measure the total current and a voltmeter to measure the voltage across one lamp. Explain one advantage of this design over a series circuit.
items.answer: Connect the 2 lamps in parallel, each branch with its own switch; put a master switch in the main circuit next to the battery. Ammeter in series in the main circuit next to the battery; voltmeter in parallel across one lamp. If one lamp fails the others stay on, and each lamp gets the full battery voltage.
items.markingKey: lamps in parallel [1]; switch on each branch [1]; master switch [1]; meters [1]; advantage [1] [5]

items.stem: In a parallel circuit, the current from the cell is …
options: equal to the sum of the currents in the branches
always less than the current in one branch
items.answer: equal to the sum of the currents in the branches
items.markingKey: Current splits at a junction and rejoins: I = I₁ + I₂.

items.stem: Explain why the current from the cell increases when another lamp is added in parallel.
items.answer: The new branch carries its own current, and the cell current is the sum of all branch currents.
items.markingKey: extra branch current [1]; total = sum [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why identical lamps in parallel are all equally bright.
items.answer: Each has the same voltage (the supply voltage) across it and so the same current.
items.markingKey: same voltage [1]; same current / brightness [1] [2]

items.stem: A 3 V battery is connected to two lamps in parallel. The ammeter next to the battery reads 0.85 A and the current in one lamp is 0.25 A. Calculate the current in the other lamp and state the voltage across it.

A 12 V battery is connected to 2 lamps in parallel. The currents in the branches are 0.1 A, 0.2 A. (a) Calculate the current from the battery. (b) State the voltage across each lamp. (c) Explain your answer to (b).
items.answer: (a) 0.3 A (b) 12 V (c) Each branch is connected directly across the battery.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.3 A [1] (b) 12 V [1] (c) branches across supply [1] [3]

items.stem: A 9 V battery is connected to 3 lamps in parallel. The currents in the branches are 0.5 A, 0.25 A, 0.2 A. (a) Calculate the current from the battery. (b) State the voltage across each lamp. (c) Calculate the resistance of the lamp carrying 0.2 A.

Ana connects a motor and a lamp in parallel to a 12 V battery. Ammeter A1 in the lamp branch reads 0.6 A and ammeter A2 in the motor branch reads 0.2 A. (a) Calculate the resistance of the component carrying the larger current. (b) Explain what happens to the current in the other branch if one component is disconnected.
items.answer: (a) 20 Ω (b) It stays the same, because its branch still has the full battery voltage.
items.markingKey: (a) R = V/I = 12/0.6 [1] = 20 Ω [1] [2] (b) unchanged [1]; same voltage [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel connects a motor and a lamp in parallel to a 9 V battery. Ammeter A1 in the lamp branch reads 0.4 A and ammeter A2 in the motor branch reads 0.5 A. (a) State the voltage across each component and explain. (b) Explain what happens to the current in the other branch if one component is disconnected. (c) Describe where to connect a voltmeter to check the voltage across one component.
items.answer: (a) 9 V across each, because each branch is connected directly across the battery. (b) It stays the same, because its branch still has the full battery voltage. (c) In parallel, directly across that component.
items.markingKey: (a) 9 V [1]; parallel branches across supply [1] [2] (b) unchanged [1]; same voltage [1] [2] (c) In parallel, directly across that component [1]

items.stem: In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is …
options: the same as the supply voltage
items.answer: the same as the supply voltage
items.markingKey: Each branch is connected directly across the supply.

items.stem: Explain why a battery runs down faster when more lamps are connected in parallel.
items.answer: The total current drawn from the battery is larger, so it transfers its energy more quickly.
items.markingKey: larger total current [1]; energy transferred faster [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the voltage across two identical lamps in series is shared equally.
items.answer: The supply voltage is divided between components in series; identical lamps get equal shares.
items.markingKey: shared in series [1]; equal for identical lamps [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a lamp with a higher resistance in a parallel branch carries a smaller current.
items.answer: All branches have the same voltage; a higher resistance allows less current for the same voltage (I = V/R).
items.markingKey: same voltage [1]; I = V/R so less current [1] [2]

items.stem: A 3 V battery is connected in series with two lamps, X and Y. The voltage across X is 1 V and the ammeter reads 0.3 A. State the voltage across Y and the current through Y.
items.markingKey: 3 − 1 = 2 V [1]; same current 0.3 A [1] [2]

items.stem: A 9 V battery is connected in series with two lamps, X and Y. The voltage across X is 2 V and the ammeter reads 0.5 A. (a) Calculate the voltage across Y. (b) State the current in Y. (c) The lamps are reconnected in parallel to the same battery. State the voltage across each lamp now.
items.answer: (a) 7 V (b) 0.5 A (c) 9 V each

items.stem: Felix connects a motor and a lamp in parallel to a 9 V battery. Ammeter A1 in the lamp branch reads 0.4 A and ammeter A2 in the motor branch reads 0.2 A. (a) Calculate the current drawn from the battery. (b) Explain what happens to the current in the other branch if one component is disconnected. (c) Describe where to connect a voltmeter to check the voltage across one component.
items.answer: (a) 0.6 A (b) It stays the same, because its branch still has the full battery voltage. (c) In parallel, directly across that component.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 A: 0.6 A [1] (b) unchanged [1]; same voltage [1] [2] (c) In parallel, directly across that component [1]

items.stem: Kenji connects a motor and a lamp in parallel to a 9 V battery. Ammeter A1 in the lamp branch reads 0.6 A and ammeter A2 in the motor branch reads 0.4 A. (a) Calculate the resistance of the component carrying the larger current. (b) Explain what happens to the current in the other branch if one component is disconnected. (c) Describe where to connect a voltmeter to check the voltage across one component.
items.answer: (a) 15 Ω (b) It stays the same, because its branch still has the full battery voltage. (c) In parallel, directly across that component.
items.markingKey: (a) R = V/I = 9/0.6 [1] = 15 Ω [1] [2] (b) unchanged [1]; same voltage [1] [2] (c) In parallel, directly across that component [1]

items.stem: Which equation links resistance R, voltage V and current I?
items.answer: R = V ÷ I
items.markingKey: Resistance = voltage ÷ current.

items.stem: Explain why increasing the resistance in a circuit reduces the current, if the voltage stays the same.
items.answer: I = V/R, so with V constant a larger R gives a smaller I; the components oppose the flow of charge more.
items.markingKey: I = V/R [1]; larger R smaller I [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a longer wire has a greater resistance.
items.answer: The electrons collide with more metal ions along a longer path, so there is more opposition to the current.
items.markingKey: longer path / more collisions [1]; more opposition [1] [2]

items.stem: A current of 2 A flows through a heating coil of resistance 1.5 Ω. Calculate the voltage across it.
items.answer: 3 V

items.stem: A current of 0.1 A flows through a lamp of resistance 15 Ω. (a) Calculate the voltage across it. (b) The voltage is changed so that the current becomes 0.2 A. Assuming the resistance is constant, calculate the new voltage.
A buzzer of resistance 90 Ω has 9 V across it. (a) Calculate the current in milliamperes (mA). (b) The voltage is halved. Assuming the resistance stays the same, state the new current and explain.
items.answer: (a) 100 mA (b) 50 mA, because I = V/R so the current is proportional to the voltage.
items.markingKey: (a) I = V ÷ R [1] = 100 mA [1] (b) 50 mA [1]; I ∝ V for constant R [1] [4]

items.stem: A technician in Lima tests a resistor and records: 1.5 V: 0.15 A, 3 V: 0.3 A, 4.5 V: 0.45 A, 6 V: 0.6 A. (a) Describe the shape of the graph of current against voltage. (b) Draw or describe the circuit used.
items.answer: (a) A straight line through the origin, showing current is proportional to voltage. (b) Cell (variable supply) in series with the resistor and an ammeter; voltmeter connected in parallel across the resistor.
items.markingKey: (a) straight line [1]; through origin [1] [2] (b) ammeter in series [1]; voltmeter in parallel [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia measures the current through a resistor at different voltages: 1.5 V: 0.375 A, 3 V: 0.75 A, 4.5 V: 1.13 A, 6 V: 1.5 A. (a) Calculate the resistance from one pair of readings. (b) Describe the shape of the graph of current against voltage. (c) Predict the current at 9 V.
items.answer: (a) 4 Ω (b) A straight line through the origin, showing current is proportional to voltage. (c) 2.25 A
items.markingKey: (a) R = V/I [1] = 4 Ω [1] [2] (b) straight line [1]; through origin [1] [2] (c) I = 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 A: 2.25 A [1]

items.stem: What is the unit of resistance?
items.answer: ohm (Ω)
items.markingKey: 1 Ω = 1 V per A.

items.stem: Explain why a thicker wire has a lower resistance.
items.answer: There is more space (more paths) for the electrons to flow through, so more current flows for the same voltage.
items.markingKey: more paths for charge [1]; lower resistance [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why heating elements are made from nichrome rather than copper.
items.answer: Nichrome has a high resistance, so it heats up a lot when current flows; it also does not oxidise easily.
items.markingKey: high resistance heats up [1]; resists oxidation / high melting point [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel says: "Resistance is the same thing as current." Explain why Daniel is wrong.
items.answer: Resistance is the opposition to current, measured in ohms; current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes.
items.markingKey: distinct definitions [1]; units [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel connects different lengths of nichrome wire to a 1.5 V cell and measures the current: 20 cm: 0.3 A, 40 cm: 0.15 A, 60 cm: 0.1 A, 80 cm: 0.075 A. Calculate the resistance of the 80 cm length.

Felix connects different lengths of nichrome wire to a 1.5 V cell and measures the current: 25 cm: 0.6 A, 50 cm: 0.3 A, 75 cm: 0.2 A, 100 cm: 0.15 A. (a) Calculate the resistance of each length. (b) Describe the relationship between length and resistance. (c) Predict the resistance of a 100 cm length.
items.answer: (a) 25 cm: 2.5 Ω, 50 cm: 5 Ω, 75 cm: 7.5 Ω, 100 cm: 10 Ω (b) Resistance is directly proportional to length (doubling length doubles resistance). (c) 10 Ω
items.markingKey: (a) resistances [1] (b) proportional [1] (c) 10 Ω [1] [3]

items.stem: Hana measures the current through a resistor at different voltages: 1.5 V: 0.188 A, 3 V: 0.375 A, 4.5 V: 0.563 A, 6 V: 0.75 A. (a) Calculate the resistance from one pair of readings. (b) Draw or describe the circuit used. (c) Explain why a filament lamp would not give a straight-line graph.
items.answer: (a) 8 Ω (b) Cell (variable supply) in series with the resistor and an ammeter; voltmeter connected in parallel across the resistor. (c) As the current increases the filament gets hotter and its resistance increases, so current rises less than proportionally.
items.markingKey: (a) R = V/I [1] = 8 Ω [1] [2] (b) ammeter in series [1]; voltmeter in parallel [1] [2] (c) filament heats [1]; resistance increases [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the purpose of a fuse?
options: To break the circuit if the current is too large
items.answer: To break the circuit if the current is too large
items.markingKey: The fuse wire melts, cutting off the current to prevent overheating and fire.

items.stem: What happens inside a fuse when the current is too large?
options: The thin wire heats up and melts
items.answer: The thin wire heats up and melts
items.markingKey: The wire melts and breaks the circuit.

items.stem: Explain how a fuse protects an appliance and its wiring.
items.answer: If a fault causes a large current, the fuse wire heats and melts, breaking the circuit before the wires overheat.
items.markingKey: large current melts fuse [1]; circuit broken before overheating [1] [2]

items.stem: A radio normally takes a current of 1 A. Fuses of 1 A, 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Choose the best fuse and explain your choice.
items.answer: 3 A: it is the smallest rating above 1 A, so it will not blow in normal use but will blow in a fault.
items.markingKey: 3 A [1]; just above normal current [1] [2]

items.stem: An engineer in Mumbai designs a safety circuit for a workshop machine that draws 2 A. The machine must run only when a safety guard is closed and the start switch is pressed. (a) Choose a fuse rating from 1 A, 3 A, 5 A and 13 A and explain your choice. (b) Suggest one further safety feature.
items.answer: (a) 3 A: the smallest rating above 2 A. (b) Use a circuit breaker, earth the metal case, or use double insulation.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 A [1]; just above working current [1] [2] (b) Use a circuit breaker, earth the metal case, or use double insulation [1]

items.stem: Where is a fuse placed in a circuit?
items.answer: In series with the appliance

items.stem: A toaster normally takes a current of 3.83 A. Fuses of 1 A, 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Choose the best fuse and explain your choice.

items.stem: Sipho designs a night light for a child’s bedroom in Singapore. It should switch on from either the door or the bed, and draws 2.5 A. (a) Choose a fuse rating from 1 A, 3 A, 5 A and 13 A and explain your choice. (b) Draw or describe a circuit diagram for the design.
items.answer: (a) 3 A: the smallest rating above 2.5 A. (b) Supply, fuse and device in series with the switch arrangement described (two switches in parallel with each other).
items.markingKey: (a) 3 A [1]; just above working current [1] [2] (b) correct switch arrangement [1]; fuse in series [1] [2]

items.stem: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
items.answer: In series with the component
items.markingKey: The current must pass through the ammeter.

items.stem: Kenji says: "Current gets used up by each lamp, so less comes back to the cell." Explain why Kenji is wrong.
items.answer: Current is not used up: the same current that leaves the cell returns to it; energy is transferred by the lamps.
items.markingKey: current not used up [1]; energy transferred [1] [2]

items.stem: A 3 V battery is connected to two lamps in parallel. The ammeter next to the battery reads 0.4 A and the current in one lamp is 0.1 A. Calculate the current in the other lamp and state the voltage across it.
A 9 V battery is connected in series with two lamps, X and Y. The voltage across X is 1.5 V and the ammeter reads 0.1 A. State the voltage across Y and the current through Y.

Kwame connects a motor and a lamp in parallel to a 6 V battery. Ammeter A1 in the lamp branch reads 0.2 A and ammeter A2 in the motor branch reads 0.3 A. (a) Calculate the resistance of the component carrying the larger current. (b) Explain what happens to the current in the other branch if one component is disconnected.
items.answer: (a) 20 Ω (b) It stays the same, because its branch still has the full battery voltage.
items.markingKey: (a) R = V/I = 6/0.3 [1] = 20 Ω [1] [2] (b) unchanged [1]; same voltage [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A lamp has 6 V across it and a current of 0.5 A. What is its resistance? (b) How does the resistance of a wire change if a thicker wire of the same material and length is used?
items.answer: (a) 12 Ω (b) It decreases
items.markingKey: (a) 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12 Ω. (b) A larger cross-sectional area gives a lower resistance.

items.stem: Sipho says: "Resistance is the same thing as current." Explain why Sipho is wrong.
items.answer: Resistance is the opposition to current, measured in ohms; current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes.
items.markingKey: distinct definitions [1]; units [1] [2]

items.stem: A student tests a nichrome wire in a circuit. The length is halved while the cross-sectional area stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the resistance changes.
items.answer: The resistance halves.
items.markingKey: Using resistance ∝ length / area: resistance ∝ length; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Yusuf connects different lengths of nichrome wire to a 1.5 V cell and measures the current: 25 cm: 0.15 A, 50 cm: 0.075 A, 75 cm: 0.05 A, 100 cm: 0.0375 A. Calculate the resistance of the 25 cm length.

Ravi connects different lengths of nichrome wire to a 1.5 V cell and measures the current: 20 cm: 0.188 A, 40 cm: 0.0938 A, 60 cm: 0.0625 A, 80 cm: 0.0469 A. (a) Calculate the resistance of each length. (b) Describe the relationship between length and resistance. (c) Predict the resistance of a 100 cm length.
items.answer: (a) 20 cm: 8 Ω, 40 cm: 16 Ω, 60 cm: 24 Ω, 80 cm: 32 Ω (b) Resistance is directly proportional to length (doubling length doubles resistance). (c) 40 Ω
items.markingKey: (a) resistances [1] (b) proportional [1] (c) 40 Ω [1] [3]

items.stem: Sofia measures the current through a resistor at different voltages: 1.5 V: 0.1 A, 3 V: 0.2 A, 4.5 V: 0.3 A, 6 V: 0.4 A. (a) Calculate the resistance from one pair of readings. (b) Predict the current at 9 V. (c) Explain why a filament lamp would not give a straight-line graph.
items.answer: (a) 15 Ω (b) 0.6 A (c) As the current increases the filament gets hotter and its resistance increases, so current rises less than proportionally.
items.markingKey: (a) R = V/I [1] = 15 Ω [1] [2] (b) I = 9 ÷ 15 = 0.6 A: 0.6 A [1] (c) filament heats [1]; resistance increases [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a two-way switch system lets a stair light be switched from the top or the bottom of the stairs.
items.answer: Each switch can connect the lamp to either of two wires; changing either switch completes or breaks the circuit.
items.markingKey: either switch changes the circuit [1]; completes or breaks path [1] [2]

items.stem: A kettle normally takes a current of 11.5 A. Fuses of 1 A, 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Choose the best fuse and explain your choice.
items.answer: 13 A: it is the smallest rating above 11.5 A, so it will not blow in normal use but will blow in a fault.
items.markingKey: 13 A [1]; just above normal current [1] [2]

items.stem: Isla designs a night light for a child’s bedroom in Seoul. It should switch on from either the door or the bed, and draws 0.5 A. (a) Explain how the fuse protects the user if a fault develops. (b) Suggest one further safety feature.
items.answer: (a) A fault causes a large current; the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, preventing overheating or electric shock. (b) Use a circuit breaker, earth the metal case, or use double insulation.
items.markingKey: (a) fuse melts with large current [1]; circuit broken [1] [2] (b) Use a circuit breaker, earth the metal case, or use double insulation [1]
